Add a chat that runs on a subscription, not an API key

Every LLM surface here was one-shot and scheduled — the nightly agent, the
recap, categorisation. None could be asked a follow-up, which is the thing
you actually want when a number looks wrong: not another report, but "why
is that figure what it is".

The answer to running it without an API key turned out to be the Claude
Agent SDK, which is Claude Code as a library and authenticates the way
Claude Code does — against credentials already on the machine, which for a
Pro or Max subscriber is the subscription. Verified with
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY explicitly deleted from the environment: it answered
correctly from real balances, held multi-turn context, and never touched a
key.

The honest position on the other providers, since the question was asked
about all three: Gemini has no login but AI Studio issues a free-tier key;
OpenAI has no path at all, because a ChatGPT subscription does not include
API access and the two are billed separately; Ollama needs no account
whatsoever and is already running here.

Being Claude Code, the SDK arrives with a filesystem and a shell. A
conversation about grocery spending has no business reading the repo, so
every tool is denied, the Claude Code system preset is replaced, and
settingSources is empty — the owner's CLAUDE.md and permission rules stay
out of a context that should never see them.

One flaw caught before it shipped: a single provider setting for every
role. Pointing it at claude_code gives free chat and a nightly agent that
silently produces nothing, because the Agent SDK exposes no
schema-enforced output and every worker depends on one. Chat now has its
own provider, and resolveLlmSettings refuses to hand a chat-only provider
to a worker rather than letting a settings change break the agent in the
dark.

subscriptions.last_commit_message:
Release 0.9.7

**OpenVPN could not configure its own interface on macOS.** Every
connection died with "Mac OS X ifconfig failed: disallowed by
script-security setting" the moment it got that far.

ShellPilot passed `--script-security 0`. openvpn's levels are 0 (no
external programs at all), 1 (built-ins such as ifconfig only, its default)
and 2 (built-ins and user scripts). The property wanted here is "no
user-defined scripts", which is 1. 0 is stricter in a way that has nothing
to do with scripts: it also forbids the ifconfig openvpn runs to bring up
its own tun interface, so the setting meant to stop a hostile server
running programs stopped the tunnel from working at all.

1 still refuses `up`, `down`, `route-up` and every other script directive —
that is exactly the difference between 1 and 2 — so nothing the reject
rules and pull-filters protect is given up.

Why it shipped: on Linux it works. Checked on a real host as root at both
levels, and the sequence completes either way, because Linux openvpn
configures the interface through netlink and never shells out. macOS runs
/sbin/ifconfig. CI is Linux, so no test could have seen it — the same shape
as the macOS-only signing bug in 0.9.5.

This is the third failure in this chain that only appeared when someone
pressed Start, and it was legible only because 0.9.6 stopped hiding the
engine's own words behind "Something went wrong inside ShellPilot."

2184 tests.

TS-57: the supply-chain and store-interface security scans (#150) (#162)

* Add TS-57: the supply-chain and store-interface security scans (#150)

Two cases from test-plan §6.5: SEC-14 (A06 vulnerable components) and SEC-15
(injection / A03 at the store interface).

**SEC-14 is partially implemented, and the PR says so.** Its oracle has two halves and
only one is expressible here. The half that is: `pyproject.toml` declares
`dependencies = []` by design (ADR-11, NFR-SYS-06), so the shipped dependency set is
empty and "no advisory in a shipped dependency" is trivially true — what makes it stop
being true is somebody adding a dependency. Four cases assert that as set equality
against transcribed literals, plus a version floor on every dev requirement and the
absence of a lockfile nobody maintains.

The half that is not: an advisory scan needs network. §4.7's tier table has no
egress-permitted non-model tier (`live` means "makes real model calls"), and "on every
push" is a CI statement while `.github/workflows/` is `.disabled` deliberately. A scanner
tested against a vendored snapshot was considered and rejected — it proves the scanner
works while saying nothing about the dependency set, and a snapshot goes stale into a lie
that reads as truth.

**SEC-15 lands in two halves, and the PR is explicit about which is the plan's probe.**
The stated probe is behavioural — call into a real `Store` and assert the search method is
not there — so it goes in behind `writtenahead` on #10. Keyed on #10 rather than #13,
which owns `FR-STORE-08`: the discriminating question is which single blocker, resolved,
makes the test runnable and non-vacuous, and an absence assertion over a class is real the
moment #10 creates it.

The source-level scan is an addition, not a substitute. It catches what the behavioural
probe structurally cannot: a store with a clean surface can still build a `WHERE` clause
with an f-string inside a declared statement.

`tests/support/sql_scan.py` parses rather than greps, and the positive control earned its
keep immediately — it caught a chain assembled across three lines that every text-shape
rule walked straight past, which is why the walker now asserts on what reaches `execute()`
rather than only on what looks like SQL. A negative control guards the other direction: a
scanner that flags the sanctioned form is one somebody switches off.

Verified: 397 passed in the gate, 6 mutations, 6 as expected, 0 survivors.

Traces to: SEC-14, SEC-15.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Close the reviewer's nine findings on TS-57 (#150)

Five were blockers and every one was demonstrated by measurement rather than argued.
The composite the reviewer named: the walker advertised six rules, four were pinned by
nothing, and of the two that were pinned one was simultaneously too narrow to catch a
realistic injection and too coarse to leave the sanctioned form alone.

**The positive control pinned no rule.** It asserted only that *some* violation fell in
each function's line range — and every planted function is caught twice, once by its own
rule and once by the execute-argument rule. Stubbing `_looks_like_sql` to return `False`,
which disables four rules outright, left all six rows green. The parametrize now carries
the expected `kind` and asserts it, so six rows are six assertions.

**`_looks_like_sql` could not see multi-line SQL** — i.e. SQL written the normal way. It
space-padded the text and searched for `" select "`, so a keyword after a newline never
matched. Now whitespace-normalized with word-boundary patterns.

**A fully compromised store scanned clean.** Combining the above with an
execute-argument rule that read `node.args[0]` only: an attribute target, a helper
parameter, a walrus binding, a starred arg and a keyword arg all reached `execute()` with
attacker-controlled text unflagged. The rule now inspects positional *and* keyword
statements, `_scope_bindings` handles `NamedExpr` and classifies function parameters as
unverifiable, and `Starred` is refused outright.

**And it false-positived on the sanctioned form.** `_computed_names` was whole-file, so an
unrelated helper binding `stmt = raw.strip()` made every `execute(stmt)` in the module a
violation — including the shape the negative control itself wrote. `sql`, `stmt` and
`query` are the commonest identifiers in a store module, so that reds the build on the
first ordinary `M-STORE` commit; against this issue's Goal a *false* finding is worse than
a miss. Bindings are per-scope now, with one hop of alias resolution and `textwrap.dedent`
recognised, and the single negative control became five parametrized ones.

**The writtenahead limb had a hole shaped like a raw passthrough.** It read
`parameters.get("stmt", "").annotation` — which raised `AttributeError` on a differently
named parameter, and let an *unannotated* `stmt` through entirely, since
`str(Parameter.empty)` contains neither "str" nor "Statement". That is the exact A03 shape
the limb exists to catch.

Also: `is_search_name` matches stems rather than whole names (`similarity_search`,
`find_similar`, `query_by_text` all passed before); the docstring no longer claims to probe
every tier when it reflects over two Protocols; `requirements-dev.txt` option lines are
asserted absent rather than skipped, closing an `--extra-index-url` hole; the version-floor
check reads the isolated specifier rather than the raw line, so a floor in a comment no
longer counts; and the negative control writes to `tmp_path` rather than into the tree.

Verified: 402 passed in the gate, the five escapes all caught, six legitimate forms all
clean, and each blocker re-run as a mutation (scope-blindness now reds the negative control
by name).

One scar worth recording: `git checkout -- tests/support/sql_scan.py` to undo a mutation
also discarded every uncommitted fix in that file. Commit before mutating, or restore from
a copy — never from the index.

The wearable changed readiness by zero, in a field annotated "applied to readiness"

Chasing the last unreachable component found the bug. BiometricSignalCard was
the only thing that read BiometricSignal.adjustment — the field whose own type
says "-15..+5 applied to readiness" — and no route imported it. Home computed
the signal on every load and dropped it on the floor. assessReadiness never
took it. So HRV, resting heart rate and sleep duration moved the score by
exactly nothing, while lib/content.ts sold the check-in as a readiness score
"that changes what it tells you to do that day" right next to the line about
importing Garmin, Whoop and Apple Health.

Wired it the way ACWR is wired, and for the same stated reason: strain you
cannot feel belongs in the verdict, not in a second panel disagreeing with it.
The adjustment moves the score, the score picks the band, and the hard limits
still short-circuit underneath — no amount of good HRV outranks a knee at 8/10
or three hours' sleep, and a load spike still caps whatever lifted it.

All three screens that produce today's verdict now pass it: home already had
the 28-day window, the check-in was fetching today's row only, and the plan
page had no biometrics query at all. Two of three would have been worse than
none — readinessFor exists precisely so those screens cannot disagree.

Two things found on the way:

baseline() averaged whatever history it had, so on day two your norm was
yesterday and an ordinary 12% overnight HRV swing read as "under strain" for
-10 points. Harmless while nothing applied it; week one of every new watch now
that something does. Seven readings before a deviation counts. Sleep hours are
an absolute threshold, so a short night still registers from day one.

The advice says which metric cost them the points, and only when it cost them
— opening a Red day with "HRV is 14% above your norm" reads as not having read
the room. Prefixed in one wrapper rather than at each return, because
`return prefix + trainedToday ? a : b` parses as `(prefix + trainedToday) ? a
: b` and is always truthy; the first attempt at this shipped that eleven times
and a test now pins the branch.

BiometricSignalCard is deleted rather than mounted: BiometricTrends on the
dashboard shows the same three metrics with baselines, deltas and sparklines,
and does it in theme tokens instead of five hardcoded hex values that fail
contrast in light mode.

43 existing tests across readiness and biometrics passed throughout, because
none of them crossed the seam. The new ones do, and all five guards were
verified by reintroducing the bug.

fix(api.mcp): reject malformed MCP tool arguments (#1943)

Three independent argument-validation defects shared one root cause: a value was trusted without confirming it named a real, in-range option.

- CredentialStampingTool silently ignored unknown argument names, dropping a misspelled or unsupported argument and proceeding as if it were never supplied. It now derives the accepted argument names from the wrapped tool's input schema and throws an McpException naming the offenders (#1941).

fix: bound test and build output, which the bound never reached (#368)

* feat(policy): bound a command's output instead of refusing the command

A refusal costs about one extra turn. On the THOL battery enforcement
took turns from 12.6 to 20.9 and measured a task-mean 1.633x vanilla
Claude Code -- last of fifteen -- while the same build without refusals
measured 0.928. The tokens a refusal saves are smaller than the round
trip it spends, so the MECHANISM is what loses, not the policy.

A PreToolUse hook can return `updatedInput`, and the rewritten call runs.
Verified end to end in
docs/superpowers/spikes/2026-08-30-posttooluse-rewrite.md. So the same
limit can be applied for zero turns.

Bash calls the router was about to refuse now run with their output
bounded to the last 8 KB instead. Only where a refusal would actually
have happened: assist and off already let the call through untouched, and
bounding there would be a new behaviour rather than a cheaper spelling of
an existing one.

WHAT KEEPS THIS HONEST

- `pipefail`, so a failing command still reports its failure. Without it
  the pipeline reports tail's status -- always 0 -- and every failing
  test run would read as passing. That is far worse than wasted tokens:
  the model would stop debugging. Asserted by running `exit 3` through
  the rewrite.
- `tail`, not `head`. A test run puts its verdict at the end, and `head`
  closes the pipe early, which under pipefail turns a successful search
  into exit 141.
- Braces, so a compound command is bounded as one unit.
- It announces itself. The spike's model NOTICED an unannounced rewrite
  and distrusted the output; a model that distrusts its output re-runs
  the command and spends the turn this exists to save.
- Five shapes are never rewritten -- heredocs, backgrounding, existing
  redirection, an author's own bound, and streaming commands -- because
  wrapping those changes what the command MEANS.

The tests RUN the rewritten commands rather than pattern-matching the
generated string, which would pass equally for a rewrite that breaks
every command it touches.

`enforcement.test.mjs` asserted `deny` for two Bash dumps. The guarantee
is unchanged and now proved against the command that will actually run,
which is stronger than a decision string -- but it is a trade and the
tests say so: a refusal let zero bytes through, a bound lets the tail
through.

Full suite: 3,248 passed. eslint: 0 errors.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* test(bench): a local debug-loop harness, and what it says

Debug loops decide the ranking -- ours measured 1.248 against tokenade's
0.611, and closing that gap alone moves the aggregate from 0.928 to
0.811. The only instrument for it was THOL, at ~$13 and an hour per
screen, which is far too coarse a loop to design against. This runs the
same shape locally, deterministically, and free: it breaks a real source
file, runs the repository's own jest three times as an agent would, and
counts the tokens each strategy would put in front of the model.

IT MEASURES THE PREMISE FIRST. Dedup rests on consecutive runs being
nearly identical, and nobody had measured "nearly". They share 94.1% of
their lines, so the premise holds.

Measured on `jest tests/hooks`, against the client's real behaviour:

  raw        20852   1.000   the client's own 30k middle truncation
  control    13417   0.643   ANSI stripped, nothing else
  bounded     3697   0.177   the 8 KB tail this project now applies
  deduped     7662   0.367   new lines only
  combined    2420   0.116   both

THE SURPRISE IS `control`. Stripping ANSI colour -- pure presentation, no
information, no risk -- removes 36% of the tokens on its own. A real
failing run measured 67,634 bytes carrying 3,080 escape sequences: 22.5%
of the BYTES but 36% of the TOKENS, because escape sequences tokenise
badly. That lever was not in the plan and costs nothing.

THREE MEASUREMENT DEFECTS WERE FOUND AND FIXED WHILE WRITING THIS, all of
which flattered the result:

  - The dedup arms were built from normalised text while the control arms
    used the raw capture, silently crediting dedup with a saving no arm
    had performed.
  - Normalisation conflated ANSI stripping (safe, shippable, worth 36%)
    with timing masking (lossy, worth 0.2%). They are now separate:
    colour is stripped in output, timings are masked only as a key for
    deciding whether two lines are the same line.
  - The baseline modelled the client as truncating from the tail. It
    truncates from the MIDDLE -- the binary carries both
    "... [N characters truncated] ..." and "truncate-middle" -- so it
    keeps the head, where the FAIL list is.

That last one is a warning about our own bound rather than about the
harness: an 8 KB tail is cheaper than the client's default AND drops the
head the client would have kept. Cost is not the only axis, and this
measures only cost.

Two further hazards are recorded in the file: dedup can hide a persistent
failure, which costs correctness rather than tokens, and 94% redundancy
is what THIS suite does when THIS file breaks.

The source file is restored in a `finally` and the restore is verified by
hash, because a benchmark in this project has already overwritten
package.json once.

Full suite: 3,248 passed.

* fix(policy): three defects the adversarial pass found in the bound

All three were live in the merged-ready branch, and each one is worse
than the token cost the module exists to reduce.

1. IT BROKE WORKING COMMANDS. The group was closed with `; }`, and two
   ordinary shapes are syntax errors under it while running fine
   unwrapped:

     echo hi # explain  ->  { echo hi # explain; }   the `; }` is inside
                            the comment, so the group never closes
     echo hi;           ->  { echo hi;; }            `;;` is a syntax error

   Both now use a newline before `}`, which terminates a comment and
   satisfies bash's separator requirement. Breaking a command that would
   have worked is the worst thing this module can do: the failure reads
   as the user's own command being wrong.

2. IT DROPPED THE HEAD THE CLIENT WOULD HAVE KEPT. The bound was
   tail-only, but Claude Code caps Bash output at 30,000 characters and
   truncates from the MIDDLE -- its binary carries both
   "... [N characters truncated] ..." and "truncate-middle". So an 8 KB
   tail was cheaper than the client's default AND lost the head, where a
   failing jest run lists which suites failed. It could have read as a
   cost win while being a regression for the model. Now keeps both ends.

3. THE MARKER LIED ON SHORT OUTPUT. `head; printf marker; tail` printed
   "middle omitted" unconditionally, announcing a truncation that never
   happened on any command under the bound -- the same class of error as
   reporting a windowed event log that was not windowed. A model told its
   output was cut goes looking for the rest, spending the turn this
   module exists to save. The marker is now gated on `read -r -N1`
   actually finding a byte after the head.

Exit status still survives all of it: `exit 3` and `exit 7` are asserted
through the two-stage pipe. The pipe stage is a GROUP rather than a bare
`head`, because a bare `head -c` exits early and SIGPIPEs the producer,
which under pipefail turns a successful command into exit 141.

* fix: address review on the bound and the debug-loop harness

   the arm was credited with the 36% that colour-stripping is worth on

* fix(policy): stop pipefail leaking into the caller's own pipeline

`pipefail` is a SHELL option, not a property of one pipe, so enabling it
for our bound changed the meaning of any command that already contained
a pipe. Measured: `false | true` exits 0 unwrapped and exited 1 once
wrapped. Silently changing a command's exit status is the same defect as
masking one, in the other direction -- and this one is worse, because it
invents a failure where the user's command had none.

The command now runs inside a subshell that restores the shell default
(`set +o pipefail`), while the OUTER pipeline -- ours -- keeps it. Both
properties hold at once:

  false | true          0 unwrapped, 0 wrapped
  true | false          1 unwrapped, 1 wrapped
  echo x; exit 3        3 unwrapped, 3 wrapped   (bound still cannot mask)
  seq 1 2000; exit 7    7 unwrapped, 7 wrapped

An explicit `set -o pipefail` written by the caller still takes effect,
because it runs inside that subshell after the reset -- asserted, so the
fix cannot be mistaken for "pipefail is now always off".

Full suite: 3,264 passed. eslint: 0 errors. sync:hooks:check clean.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(policy): drop the truncation probe, which lied and was not portable

Two review findings, and the fix for both is to DELETE the mechanism
rather than patch it a third time.

The in-stream marker had already been wrong twice. Unconditional, it
announced an omission for every output that fitted. Gated on
`read -r -N1`, it narrowed the lie to outputs between half the bound and
the bound itself -- where `head` takes its half, `tail` takes the entire
remainder, nothing is dropped, and an omission was still announced. The
probe also relied on a bash-only `read -N`: a POSIX shell rejects it, so
the `if` body was skipped, the tail never printed, and the error leaked
to stderr because only the `pipefail` probe was redirected.

Both defects have the same root: a pipe cannot detect truncation it has
not yet consumed. So the detection is gone.

`{ head -c H; tail -c H; }` is already exact in every regime, which is
what made the marker unnecessary in the first place:

  total <= half        head prints it all, tail has nothing  -> COMPLETE
  half < total <= max  head takes half, tail takes the rest  -> COMPLETE
  total > max          head takes half, tail takes the last  -> exactly max

Verified at all three sizes, byte for byte against the unwrapped command.

The announcement moves into `boundNotice` and is now stated as the POLICY
-- "anything over N bytes is returned as its beginning and its end,
shorter output is returned complete" -- rather than as a claim about this
particular output. A policy statement is true whether or not this command
was cut, so it cannot lie, and the model still knows what is being done
to it.

The emitted command is now POSIX shell: no `read -N`, no bashism beyond
the `pipefail` probes, which are already redirected and optional.

* fix(policy): clustered follow flags, and the caller's own pipefail state

Two findings, and the second is the previous fix mirrored.

CLUSTERED SHORT OPTIONS. GNU tail accepts `-fn 1` and `-fF`, and a guard
anchored on `-f\b` matches neither: the word boundary fails against the
next letter in the cluster. Both keep following and never reach EOF, so
the bound waits forever and the hook returns no tool result at all. The
guard now looks for f or F anywhere in a short-option cluster, and the
opposite direction is still asserted -- `tail -n 5` and `tail -c 100`
must remain boundable, or the fix has over-corrected.

commit stopped our `pipefail` leaking into the caller's pipelines by
hard-clearing it in the subshell. That is the same bug mirrored: a caller
running under `bash -o pipefail` gets 1 from `false | true`, and the hard
clear handed them 0. Either direction is a silent change to an exit
status we were only supposed to be bounding the output of.

`set +o` prints the current options in re-inputtable form, so the
`pipefail` line is captured before anything changes and eval'd back
inside the subshell. Asserted in both shells:

  bash            false | true   0 plain, 0 bounded
  bash -o pipefail false | true  1 plain, 1 bounded
  bash            echo x; exit 3 3 plain, 3 bounded

* fix(hooks): we were blind to web calls, and half the product never installed

Two weaknesses, found by asking where the benchmark says we are weakest
and then looking at whether we even receive the events.

1. WE NEVER SAW A WEB CALL

The PreToolUse matcher listed Read|Grep|Glob|Edit|MultiEdit|Write|Bash|

reached the router, `decide()` had no branch for them, and 4,499 recorded

That is the family THOL says decides the board. web-research-oss-inventory

leader scores 0.325 on it against our nothing.

Both matchers now include the web tools, and a repeated WebFetch of a URL
this session already fetched is COLLAPSED rather than refused: the call
proceeds with a rewritten prompt, so the page is not sent again and no
turn is spent. WebFetch answers its prompt with a small model, so a
shorter prompt is a shorter result. Session-scoped, and the wording says
so -- the page may genuinely have changed, and the only claim made is
"you already asked this session", which is a fact we hold rather than an
inference about the page.

carried three events. The plugin manifest carries five. So every script
install ran without:

                eager staleness marking
  Stop          NO HARVEST AT ALL -- the learning half never ran, so the
                knowledge graph stayed empty however long the session was

never invoked on one of them, which is why it survived: a hook that is
never called is indistinguishable from a hook that decides to do nothing.

Nothing compared the two lists. `sync:hooks:check` verifies that the
vendored hook SOURCES match hooks-core and says nothing about which
events an install registers, so the drift was invisible to every gate.

and matcher by matcher, and it caught the PostToolUse/Stop gap on its
first run rather than being written to fit what was already there.

Two existing wire tests had to move with the change, and neither was
weakened: Stop could no longer stand for "an event we do not touch", so
the fixture gained Notification for that role and a new case asserts the
user's own Stop hook survives beside ours; and a hardcoded
`preserving == 2` is now derived from the fixture, because a literal
there asserts the fixture rather than the behaviour.

package version never bumped. Comparing them measured two days of build
changes as if they were the schema tax, and the giveaway was in the
buckets: output tokens fell 30% and turns fell, which a fixed prefix
cost cannot cause. The stale rows were purged and every arm re-run on
one tree.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(hooks): never bound a command's first run

The bound was net-negative and the measurement said why. With the product
actually on (MODE=assist, no MCP), SEG_1 went 0.924 -> 1.273 against
control and the debug segment's turns to 2.305: code-debug-pipeline-py
22 -> 31 turns, code-debug-ledger-py 15 -> 24, code-debug-cascade-py
28 -> 39. The model could not see which test failed, so it ran the
command again, and a round trip costs far more than the bytes the bound
saved. Our bound is 8,000 bytes where the client already truncates at
30,000, so we were cutting 3.75x harder than the host.

Cutting output the model has NEVER SEEN is the whole problem. On a
repeat it has already read the full text, so bounding costs it nothing
it did not already have -- and the compactor keeps the ending intact and
emits lines that are new, so a failure that changed still arrives. The
first run of any command now goes through untouched; the client's own
30,000 cap still applies, so the worst case is the baseline.

The counter-example is why this is a rule about WHEN rather than a
retreat: code-comprehension-django went 2 -> 19 turns and still cost
0.456, because control dumped an enormous context in two turns and we
replaced it with nineteen cheap ones. Bounding is not wrong; withholding
what the model needs to act is.

Three defects found while building it, all of which failed silently:

- Seen-tracking first read the compactor's previous-output file, so
  TOKEN_OPTIMIZER_COMPACT=0 -- documented as the escape hatch that
  restores the shell stage -- switched bounding off entirely. The marker
  is now its own file, independent of compaction.
- markSeen referenced a `dirname` that was never imported. Both callers
  wrap the state work in try/catch, so the ReferenceError was swallowed
  and the feature was simply off. The parent directory is known, so the
  import is gone rather than added.
- stateDir was a `const` arrow declared below the router's main flow,
  which runs at module top level: function declarations hoist, consts do
  not, so it was in the temporal dead zone and every call threw into the
  same silent catch. It is a function declaration now.

Each of those produced "bounding quietly does nothing" with no error
anywhere, which is only visible by checking the state directory rather
than the exit code.

Tests updated to the new contract rather than around it: the router
helpers seed the marker the compactor's pipe stage would have written,
so cases about what the bound DOES still exercise it, and four new cases
pin the rule itself -- first run untouched, repeat bounded, a different
command not treated as seen, and no carry-over between sessions. Those
use per-run session ids, because the markers live in the OS temp
directory and outlive the process: fixed ids passed once and then failed
for the rest of the day.

* fix(hooks): stop telling the model that tools which do not exist are available

session-start.mjs did

  process.env.TOKEN_OPTIMIZER_MCP_CAPABILITIES ??= HOOK_MCP_TOOLS.join(',')

on the grounds that the plugin owns both this hook and its MCP
declaration, so the tools must exist. They need not. The hooks install
without the server on the script path, a user can keep the hooks and
drop the server, and the benchmark arm that removes the mcp block does
exactly that. In each case the fabricated list was persisted as PROVEN
evidence and the model was told at session start that nine optimizer
tools were available.

The instructions are the damage, not the claim. It told the model to
call optimize_session when context is tight, to use
get_optimization_report, and -- at length -- to call wiki_write whenever
it worked something out. With no server those calls fail and get
retried, and the wiki_write direction asks for work the task never
wanted, which costs turns whether the tool exists or not.

The shape of it was the giveaway once measured: with the host declaring
five real tools this hook injects 338 characters and names none of them;
with NO server at all it injected 1,403 and named three that do not
exist. The no-evidence path was four times larger AND wrong. It is now
352 characters, claims nothing, and names nothing, while the host-
declared path is untouched at 338.

decide.mjs already stated the rule this violated: production never
converts install intent into a claim that an MCP tool exists.

This is a candidate cause for the measured turn inflation (SEG_1 1.48x,
SEG_4 2.23x), not a confirmed one -- the run that tests it comes next.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix(hooks): assert the bundled tool inventory only for an actual plugin install

Every hook entry point ran

  process.env.TOKEN_OPTIMIZER_MCP_CAPABILITIES ??= <bundled list>

unconditionally. That is right for a plugin, where .mcp.json travels with
the hooks, and wrong everywhere else: the script path wires hooks through
settings.json without the server, a user can drop the server and keep the
hooks, and the benchmark arm removes the mcp block outright. In those
cases the fabricated list was persisted as PROVEN evidence and the model
was told to call tools that do not exist.

Measured over a debug-sized task with no server: post-tool alone emitted
3,450 characters built on the assumption, including "Call the
token-optimizer MCP tool smart_read" after every repeated read -- a
failed call and a retry each time, on a benchmark where turns dominate
cost. Total hook injection over 18 calls drops 7,466 -> 4,016 characters
with no phantom tool named anywhere.

CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT tells the two apart: the plugin runtime sets it, a
settings.json install does not. Verified both ways -- with it, session
start still injects 1,403 characters naming the tools, which is the
tested plugin behaviour; without it, 352 and nothing named.

THIS REVERSES A DELIBERATE, TESTED DECISION, so it is scoped rather than
removed. mcp-capability-negotiation.test.mjs pins "plugin enforces its
bundled MCP tools without host inventory" and now sets CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT
to state the premise its own name claims; without that it was silently
exercising the settings path instead.

The doctor needed the same care and would have regressed silently: it is
a CLI run outside the plugin runtime, so it never has CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT
and its enforcement probe would have reported "not refused" for a
correctly installed plugin -- a false negative in the one tool whose job
is to tell the user the truth. Its probe now supplies the inventory
explicitly, because the question it asks is whether enforcement would
fire if the tools were there.

Found because post-tool.mjs and stop.mjs are GENERATED: an edit to them
was silently reverted by the next sync:hooks, and only the generator in
scripts/generate-client-entries.mjs actually changes them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* feat(hooks): point a large read at an outline of the same file

Tokenade reaches 0.666 context-per-turn by offering compact views --
skeleton, query, map -- through a CLI the agent must CHOOSE to call,
taught by a project rules file loaded on every task whether it helps or
not. That fixed cost is why their advantage scales with task length
(corr -0.689) and why they lose the three shortest tasks outright.

We sit in the tool path rather than beside it. PreToolUse can rewrite a
Read's file_path, so the substitution happens inside a call the model
already made: no CLI, no rules file, no schema, nothing to adopt, and
nothing paid on a short task. Measured through the real router:
src/server/index.ts 97KB -> 0.9KB, hooks-core/decide.mjs 43KB -> 1.5KB,
package.json untouched because it has no outline worth having.

A RE-READ IS NOT A LOSS, which is what makes this safe where the output
bound was not. A 50KB file read in full sits in context and is re-read
every later turn; an outline plus one TARGETED read of the region it
names is about 4KB. A turn costs ~$0.01 and cache_read is $0.30/M, so a
turn is worth ~33k tokens of re-reading -- about 2.2k tokens saved across
15 remaining turns. That arithmetic is where the floor comes from, and
why it RISES as a session runs out of turns to amortise over: ~8KB at
turn 2, ~29KB at turn 12, and no substitution at all near the end.

The outline carries signatures and line numbers, not just names. A bare
name list would send the model back to the file to learn what something
takes, which is the re-read this exists to avoid.

Also: DEFAULT_BOUND_BYTES 8,000 -> 30,000, the client's own cap. Cutting
3.75x harder than the host is what drove the model to re-run commands
(debug segment 1.279, turns 2.305). Matching it means the worst case is
the baseline, and the value moves from truncating to compacting repeats.

Two defects caught while building, both of the kind that fail silently:
extractImports was called but never imported, so a catch swallowed the
ReferenceError and the fallback regex ran instead; and substitutionFor
reached statSync without isFsSafePath, which a Read payload carrying an
invalid code point turns into a libuv ABORT rather than a catchable
error. The existing libuv test caught the second.

* fix(ios): honour the user's reading voice; fix the wrapped position label

Peter, on build 35: "It is the correct language now but not the voice I have
selected. It sounds like the regular Siri voice although I have downloaded
premium voices and configured it." And: the player buttons are too small and
too close, and "6" over "…" is unexplained.

WHAT HIS PHONE ACTUALLY LOADED, read from its speech log over WiFi:
`com.apple.voice.premium.en-AU.Karen`. The right tier, the wrong voice — Siri's
Australian voice, which is exactly what "the regular Siri voice" was. The
ranking chose the best quality tier and then picked ARBITRARILY among equals.

THERE IS NO API FOR "THE VOICE THE USER PICKED IN SETTINGS". Measured on
macOS with the same API: `AVSpeechSynthesisVoice(language:)` returns the
compact voice no matter what is installed or selected, and an utterance with
no voice follows the DEVICE language. So the app has to remember the choice
itself — and honour it.

  language in `mobile-store.speechVoices`, applied live (the current paragraph

  joke set (`com.apple.speech.synthesis.voice.*` — Albert, Bad News, Bells,
  Zarvox…) and the Eloquence screen-reader family are 19 of the 25 English

inside the fixed-height host and truncated — `.lineLimit(1)` + `.fixedSize()`
and required compression resistance on the host view. Buttons 48/56pt with
8pt spacing, up from 44/48 and 2pt.

Show a saved crop everywhere, not only in the editor that made it (#1087)

The serious half of #1085 §1a. Saving a crop appeared to do nothing:
the photo stayed in its original framing everywhere in the app.

The recipe was saved correctly, but only PhotoTransformsView rendered a
photo through it. Every other surface loaded /photos/file/<filename> —
the untouched original: every grid, album, timeline and feed tile, the
fullscreen viewer, the slideshow, the collage preview and its export. So
the edit was visible inside the sheet that made it and nowhere else,
which reads as the crop never having been applied.

A photo the signed-in user has a recipe for is now fetched from
GET /photos/:id/render?v=user instead. Which photos those are comes from
GET /photos/transforms/mine — one call for the whole app, held in
TransformedPhotosIndex, the way the web's useTransformedPhotosIndex
does it. The set is patched in place when this app saves, adopts or
resets a recipe, so an edited photo changes over at once.

The cache key was the trap. ImageCache is disk-backed, so "photo-<file>"
would have kept serving the pre-edit pixels across relaunches. Every key
now carries the user and a per-photo revision, and the revision travels
in the query too: the render route answers Cache-Control: immutable, so
an unchanged URL would have let URLSession hold the old bytes as well.
Photos without a recipe keep exactly the key they have today, so no
existing cache is thrown away on update.

Two places deliberately keep the original: a fullscreen page drawing a
face box (the box is in the original's coordinates) and the download
service that writes to the device library (the original is the archival
copy). Where a recipe is rendered, the AI's focal point is dropped —
the user's own framing is the answer to what the photo is of.

Known gap: an edit made elsewhere bumps no revision here, so a *second*
edit to an already-edited photo made on the web can be served from this
phone's cache until it is evicted. The first recipe on a photo always
shows, because that flips the photo out of the index.

GSE2065: guard the probe-name collision, and correct the array-vector note

Checking Dittmar et al.'s Table 1 (EMBO Rep 2005, PMC1299251) settles the
manuscript's relative array vector: (0.086, 0.042, 0.039, 0.24, 0.21) and the
Northern (0.024, 0.025, 0.017, 0.19, 0.11) are BOTH published values, and the
Figure 4C baselines match Appendix B exactly. The earlier note here calling the
array vector unreconciled was wrong in what it implied -- a published summary
was never going to fall out of the deposit. The ~13% gap is what Appendix B
already predicts: GEO carries no raw channel signals, so the internal-amine
correction can be neither applied nor removed.

The real finding is the collision it exposed. GPL1746 is a MULTI-SPECIES array.
Dittmar et al. label their five E. coli groups Leu-1..Leu-5; on the platform
those names belong to Bacillus subtilis probes (trnD-Leu2, trnB-Leu2, trnS-Leu1,
trnJ-Leu2, trnJ-Leu1), with Leu-11..Leu-14 being S. cerevisiae. Only Leu-6..
Leu-10 are E. coli. Mapping the paper's labels onto the deposit by name analyses
B. subtilis and reports it as E. coli leucine charging -- no error raised, five
plausible trajectories, a plausible error floor.

Going through Entrez GeneIDs rather than names is what avoided it, so that is now
pinned rather than left as a stylistic choice:
test_groups_come_from_the_ecoli_probes_not_the_paper_labels asserts the exact
correspondence and that no B. subtilis or yeast probe is ever grouped, so a later
"fix" aligning probe names with the manuscript fails loudly.

1123 passed, ruff clean.

subscriptions.last_commit_message:
fix(app): never show a raw exception's own text to the user (#74)

Real bug, found from a live screenshot: tapping a Submit-screen field
picker while the backend was unreachable showed a raw caught exception's
toString() straight in a SnackBar — "ClientException with
SocketException: Connection reset by peer ..., address =
spekooh-staging.onrender.com, port = 42216, uri=...". That's the backend's
real hostname and port, plus internal socket/OS error details, shown
directly to a user in French, over what should have been a friendly
"couldn't load, try again" message.

Traced the same `l10n.xxxError('$e')` anti-pattern (interpolating a caught
exception's own text into a user-facing string) to 10 call sites across 5
files: submit_screen.dart (x3), paper_detail_screen.dart (x4),
edit_profile_sheet.dart, paywall_sheet.dart. Every one is a generic
`catch (e)` after any more specific typed exception is already handled,
so what actually reaches it is either an ApiException (an HTTP response
did come back) or a raw network/parsing failure (nothing came back at
all) — the exact SocketException case from the screenshot.

Added apiErrorDetail(Object) in api_client.dart: extracts the backend's
own curated `detail` message from an ApiException's JSON body (safe to
show — every one of this codebase's error responses wraps one of its own
hand-authored domain exceptions, e.g. PaperUnlockError("Already
unlocked."), never a raw system exception; verified this against all 15
open "information exposure through an exception" CodeQL alerts at the
time — every one is the same false-positive pattern, str(exc) on a
curated custom exception, not a real leak. No backend code change needed;
left a note for the owner to dismiss those 15 alerts as false positives
in GitHub's Security tab, with the reasoning to paste in). Returns null
for anything else — a non-JSON body, a missing detail field, or a raw
exception with no ApiException wrapper at all — so callers fall back to
AppLocalizations.authErrorUnknown (an existing, already-localized generic
message) instead of ever surfacing raw exception text.

Also fixed a small, real UX inconsistency spotted in the same screenshot:
Submit's field-picker rows showed "Choisir"/"Choose" as a placeholder for
an enabled field but a bare "-" for a disabled one (Type d'examen/Matière
before their prerequisite is picked) — inconsistent and uninformative
next to otherwise-identical rows. Both now show the same placeholder
text; the already-dimmed chevron alone signals "not tappable yet".

Testing: new api_client_error_test.dart unit-tests apiErrorDetail against
a real backend error body, a non-JSON body, a JSON body with no detail
field, and a raw exception — confirming it only ever extracts the safe
case. New end-to-end widget test in submit_quizzes_screens_test.dart
reproduces the exact screenshot's failure (a repository throwing that
same SocketException text) and asserts the resulting SnackBar contains
neither the hostname nor "SocketException", only the generic fallback —
confirmed this fails against the pre-fix code before restoring the fix.
flutter analyze clean, full app suite passes (177/177). A full release
APK also builds successfully with these fixes included.

which imports app.core.compat, which imports structlog at module level. The
pip line named what the test file imports, not what importing it executes;
the local venv has everything, so no local run could show the gap.

  import chain statically from the CSP test file through every app.* module
  and package __init__ it reaches, and fails when the workflow line's
  packages (plus their transitive closure per local metadata) do not provide

feat(encode): self-contained KEY-frame encode with NO C bootstrap; 9/9 byte-exact

Adds the missing outer shell. Before this, every encoder path in the repo ran
real libaom FIRST and built on its output: aom-bench's port_encode takes a
bootstrap and parses C's sequence + frame headers, and avif_parity splices C's
sequence-header OBU bytes verbatim in front of the port's frame OBU.
write_sequence_header_obu was byte-exact but had ZERO call sites in any
crates/*/src. The search / transform / entropy / pack layers were never the
gap; the shell was.

New: aom_encode::key_frame::encode_key_frame(planes, cfg) -> Result<Vec<u8>>
returns a complete temporal unit (TD OBU + sequence-header OBU + OBU_FRAME)
with no C bytes in the path. Everything is derived:
  - seq_level_idx/tier via the new aom_encode::seq_level (set_bitstream_level
    _tier, encoder.c:464), lifted out of seq_level_idx_diff.rs where a prior
    session had parked it; the test now calls it instead of duplicating it.
  - profile / bit depth / subsampling / num_bits_* / the reduced-still-picture
    framing from init_seq_coding_tools (encoder.c:587).
  - base_qindex from rc::base_qindex_from_cq.
  - allow_screen_content_tools from screen_detect (av1_set_screen_content
    _options), not read off a header.
  - the tile grid from av1_get_tile_limits + av1_calculate_tile_cols/rows.
  - loop-filter levels from pick_filter_level on THIS port's own recon.
  - the tx_mode SELECT->LARGEST flip (encodeframe.c:2797) from a new
    txb_split_count over the port's own winner trees, so phase 2 packs the
    final header mode while search_tx_mode_is_select keeps the tx-size CDF
    adapting as the search's did (KB-42's split).

CORRECTION to the coverage audit: COVERAGE.md row 1.4 names
av1_get_seq_level_idx as "the ONE true missing header ALGORITHM". It is the
wrong target -- that function computes the ACHIEVED level from accumulated
AV1LevelInfo stats and runs only under keep_level_stats, which is 0 by
default; the WRITTEN header level comes from set_bitstream_level_tier. The
prior session that wrote seq_level_idx_diff.rs had already found this; the
finding is now in the module docs where it cannot be missed.

Gate: aom-encode/tests/self_contained_key_frame.rs, 5 tests.
  - 9/9 cells BYTE-IDENTICAL to real aomenc's whole temporal unit (mono/420/
    422/444, 64x64 / 128x64 / 128x96 / 128x128, cq 10/24/32/40/55, flat +
    textured), 18..621 bytes each.
  - both decoders (real aom_codec_av1_dx and this repo's aom-decode) decode
    the port's own stream to the pixels real aomenc's stream decodes to, 9/9.
  - the gap is MEASURED, not asserted: strip the sequence header from the
    port's own stream and the real C decoder refuses it (18 -> 10 bytes).
  - mutation proof: a one-field change (cq 32 -> 52 spliced behind the
    unmutated sequence header) makes BOTH the byte gate and the pixel gate go
    red, so neither is vacuous.
  - the shell REFUSES what it has no gate for by name (CDEF on, LR on, speed
    != 0, usage != ALLINTRA, wrong plane sizes, a frame whose tile limits
    mandate a split) instead of silently mis-encoding.

Also documents avif_parity.rs plainly as NOT an end-to-end gate -- it runs C
first and copies C's sequence header -- so it cannot be read as one again.

Named and NOT wired (module docs carry the entry points): CDEF on, loop
restoration on, multi-tile, av1_determine_sc_tools_with_encoding's trial
encode, speeds > 0, bit depths > 8, SB128.

Fix chosenIds() under-selecting: 1 stream instead of AUTO_FALLBACK_DEPTH

Reported via Discord: a channel pushed with only one stream in its
Dispatcharr failover list despite several clean candidates being
ranked. Root cause: chosenIds()'s last-resort fallback (used whenever
a channel's selection has neither `streams` nor `primary` set -- the
normal state for any channel that's only ever had a wantlist [Group]
header carried into it, i.e. most freshly-run channels) returned just
the single top candidate, while autoPick() and the server's own push
fallback (_resolve_curated) both default to AUTO_FALLBACK_DEPTH (4).

The mismatch was invisible until something persisted it: a drag, a
digit key, an Add-then-Remove -- any of those baked the shown (wrong,
1-item) list into selection.json, permanently narrowing what would
otherwise have been a 4-deep automatic failover chain down to one
stream. Fixed to match AUTO_FALLBACK_DEPTH exactly. Also fixed a
stale UI label found investigating the same report: "Native (one
channel, two streams)" undersold what that mode actually does (an
ordered list of any length), leftover text from before that was true.

Channels already narrowed to one stream by this bug before the fix
won't self-heal -- selection.json already has an explicit short
`streams` list for them. Only affects channels never touched again
after being narrowed.

fix(proxy): stop maskProxyUrl leaking passwords, repair test-all output (v1.12.2)

Found by pointing the proxy tooling at a real 10-proxy vendor list rather
than at the fixtures, then carrying that configuration into .env.test.

maskProxyUrl() could return a password in clear text. A URL whose userinfo
did not survive parsing was returned verbatim, and a URL is easy to get into
that state: omitting the scheme makes user:pw@host:8080 parse as the *scheme*
"user:", stranding the password in the path where nothing masked it. That is
an easy mistake to make given the TXT list format is itself scheme-less.
Every proxy string the CLI prints, error text included, routes through this
one function, so the leak reached anywhere a malformed proxy was reported.
Userinfo is now redacted on both the parse-success and parse-failure paths;
a string with no "@" is still returned untouched, since it has no userinfo to
hide and mangling it would remove the detail explaining the failure.

scrub() replaced every literal occurrence of the password anywhere in a
message, so a one-character password of "p" rendered "before receiving
CONNECT response" as "... res****onse". Userinfo is now replaced
unconditionally, and the blanket replacement kept only as a backstop for
passwords long enough (8+) that colliding with prose is implausible.

HPE_* CONNECT failures now carry a hint. Vendors that reject bad credentials
by writing a response and closing the socket never reach the 407 branch, and
surfaced as "Parse Error: Data after `Connection: close`" - the parser's
problem, not the operator's.

Three display defects, all with correct --json already, so deploy gating was
never affected:

- proxy test-all --ip collected exit IPs and rendered no column for them, so
  the flag cost a round trip per proxy and showed nothing.
- test-all rows were indistinguishable on real vendor lists. The masked URL
  at width 40 truncated identically on every row when a pool shares one long
  username, and rows sort by latency, so nothing identified the slow proxy.
  Rows are now host:port, which both differs and carries no credentials.
  Over-long endpoints keep their tail, because a per-session port is often
  the only thing separating two entries.
- instance status rejected an instance that instance ls lists, breaking the
  documented pin-then-create workflow.

Also corrects docs/PROXY.md, which claimed the deterministic strategy spreads
N instances across N proxies. Rendezvous hashing is stateless and collides:
10 instances over a 10-proxy pool resolve to about 7 distinct egress IPs.

The two "no proxy file configured" tests now unset MIAW_PROXY_FILE around
themselves - it is a setting operators are told to export, and it silently
satisfied the condition under test, so those failed on exactly the machines
using the feature and passed in CI.

feat(learning): WikiSkill adaptation — persistent wiki layer, skill-impact ledger, validation gates

Root cause / why: Google's WikiSkill (arXiv:2608.27454, Aug 2026) shows
agent skill evolution works best as a three-layer loop — immutable traces,
a never-resetting distilled wiki, and rollback-able skills — with two
mechanisms Atom lacked: an acceptance ledger so evolvers never re-propose
rejected mutations, and validation gates on skill promotion. Ablations
also show the runtime agent must NOT read raw wiki knowledge (63.7→60.9),
and that weak-model skills transfer catastrophically (50.5%→18.1%).

What landed (docs/architecture/WIKISKILL_ADAPTATION_PLAN.md):
- W1 skill_impact_entries + core/auto_dev/skill_impact_ledger.py: every
  UnifiedEvolutionPipeline outcome (accept/reject@gate/rollback) appends;
  Memento/AlphaEvolver generation prompts render the acceptance history.
- W2/W3 knowledge_patterns + core/knowledge_pattern_service.py: the wiki
  layer. Sleep-time maintainer (new step 5 in exchange_memory_maintenance)
  samples ≤5 failing + ≤3 passing traces (first loop here to mine passing
  traces) and distills failure modes/success strategies — LLM when
  reachable, deterministic fallback (tool-error signatures + rated
  episodes) so the wiki grows offline. Evolver prompts read the index.
- W4 pinned: memory_context_assembler gains no wiki leg (import-graph
  test); wiki knowledge reaches inference only as compiled
  lessons/playbooks.
- W5 ATOM_PLAYBOOK_EVAL_GATE (off|shadow|enforce, default shadow):
  PlaybookService.approve() replays a draft's origin incident evals before
  draft→approved; enforce blocks while any fails (skips never block);
  shadow records playbooks.last_eval_result. /api/playbooks/{id}/approve
  uses the gated path (409 on block).
- W6 transfer safety: packs carry source agent model provenance; imports
  land quarantined (experience_items.validation_state=pending); advisory
  kinds auto-activate on a clean incident-eval replay, skills wait for
  explicit review (core/experience_marketplace/transfer_safety.py +
  maintenance step 6).
- Schema: alembic 20260902_wikiskill_adaptation (Postgres);
  sqlite_schema_repair covers playbooks.last_eval_result and
  experience_items.source_model/validation_state on local SQLite.

Live-exposed pre-existing bug fixed here: exchange_maintenance_loop called
the async run_maintenance_cycle WITHOUT await — the whole sleep-time loop
(backfill/distill/auto-promote/playbook drafting) had never executed in
the live app; the log showed a bare coroutine object. Caught by the
live-app verification (scripts/wikiskill_live_check.py), fixed with
await + pinned by test_loop_awaits_the_cycle; live log now shows a real
cycle summary (playbook_drafts immediately bumped 7 stuck drafts).

Verified how: 39 new tests (ledger incl. pipeline wiring + evolver prompt
injection; pattern dedup/balance/distiller/index + W4 pin; eval gate
shadow/enforce/skip semantics + eval_ids runner filter; transfer
quarantine/activation/reimport-requarantine) + 327 total across all
touched suites green. Live on :8011: schema repair applied all three
columns, API approve returned eval_gate with a REAL eval replay (ran=1,
failed=1, shadow-approved by design), maintenance cycle ran in-app with
patterns+import_validation steps. Other agents' in-flight files untouched.

subscriptions.last_commit_message:
PosterChanOS: a slow compositor must not cost the desktop at boot

One restart came up as the ordinary single-column client and was not
reproducible by hand; that boot's log carried 'Network service crashed' and
'GPU process launch failed' from the previous instance's teardown.

restore() decides synchronously, and PCOSShell.available() is a read of _have,
which is null until the ASYNC detect() has asked the compositor. Until then the
PosterChanOS branch is skipped and the fall-through applies the remembered
osMode AND fits() -- a size check. Reproduced against the shipped os.js:

  OS · detect answered, wide    desktop=true
  OS · detect answered, narrow  desktop=true
  OS · detect PENDING, wide     desktop=true
  OS · detect PENDING, NARROW   desktop=FALSE   <- and nothing re-decides
  OS · pending, narrow, no pref desktop=FALSE

Both conditions at once is what that teardown produces: a slow socket and a
window without its real size. Every other combination is fine, which is why it
happened once. detect() is now awaited and the desktop entered when it answers.
Additive: enter() is idempotent and refuses inside a window, and a browser has
no bridge so detect resolves false -- the three browser rows are identical
before and after, asserted, not assumed.

Google Search Console "Blocked by robots.txt" result — a crawl request
landing inside the restart window gets a connection failure, and Google's
fallback for an unreachable robots.txt is to treat the whole site as
disallowed.

the Render dashboard (confirmed against the dashboard's own Settings page,
not guessed). This updates render.yaml to match, since it's the source of
truth on any future Blueprint sync — left as `free`, a sync would have

feat(paiement): la page de retour attend vraiment la confirmation

Un paiement mobile money est très souvent encore PENDING quand le
client revient sur le site : l'opérateur confirme hors bande, et
Maketou n'a pas de webhook fiable. La page ne vérifiait qu'une fois,
puis affichait "repasse dans quelques minutes" — un cul-de-sac où
plus rien ne bouge alors que la personne vient de payer.

Elle interroge maintenant la route de vérification toutes les 5 s
pendant environ 2 minutes, avec le temps écoulé à l'écran, puis passe
la main au cron de réconciliation en le disant franchement : la page
peut être fermée, la vérification continue côté serveur.

Un échec réseau ne dit rien du paiement lui-même : il est traité comme
"pas encore réglé" et laissé au tour suivant, jamais requalifié en
échec de paiement.

AND with each other.

## The command count is now a pointer, not a number

While writing this, the count went 315 -> 316: a command landed mid-session and
the test caught it immediately. That is the check working, but it also showed
the cost - a number that moves this often needs editing in three places, and
two of them are prose nobody thinks to update.

already rejects it when stale, so it is the authority. `AGENTS.md` and
`stacks-buddy` now point at it rather than restating it, and the assertions
that policed those restatements are gone. Pinning a number is right when it
moves rarely; deferring to the generated artifact is right when it does not.

`buddy setup:ai` regenerated the installed copies.

subscriptions.name: sim
subscriptions.last_commit_message:
perf(pass_a): write a run's corroborations in one round trip, not ~730

Measured over 30 runs (3 days): the pipeline averages 800s, Pass A 446s of it
(56%), and inside Pass A the three costs are article_fetch 132s, dedup CPU 110s
and corroboration_db 90s — 74% of the pass between them.

The 90s is not work, it is latency: ~730 duplicates per run, each paying its own
UPDATE against a remote pooler. load_domain_penalties already found and fixed
exactly this shape ("Measured at 210 s/run (25% of Pass A) as a per-item query —
the round trips were the cost, not the data"), so this follows it.

The refusals stay per-duplicate: _corroboration_params holds every rule
_record_corroboration applied — self-republish, carrier-not-a-witness, missing id
— so a duplicate that must not be recorded never reaches the batch, and a future
rule has one home. _record_corroboration keeps its signature and behaviour for
the three test files that cover it.

Batched with executemany rather than a single UPDATE ... FROM (VALUES ...).
psycopg3 pipelines executemany, so it is also one round trip, but the statements
still run server-side in order — which is required: the `NOT @> probe` guard
makes a second duplicate from an already-credited domain a no-op only if the
first append is visible. A VALUES join applies one row per target and would
silently drop every duplicate after the first for the same event, and with ~730
duplicates across ~100 events, most share a target.

The trade is durability: corroborations land at the end of Pass A instead of as
they are found, so a mid-loop crash loses them. Acceptable for what the module
already calls a bonus signal; the events themselves still commit as they go.
corroboration_cpu is now timed separately so the next measurement can tell the
filters apart from the write.
